lead: A domain is the set of rights a process holds at one moment, written as pairs: each object and the rights on it. It stops a process carrying its user's full power all the time. UNIX-like systems switch domains daily: passwd, sudo, containers, phone app permissions.
prereq: You need the meaning of a right from 6.1 and the process control block from Unit 2.

sections.h3: A domain is a set of pairs

blocks.text: A domain D is a set of pairs (o, r). o is an object: file, printer, memory segment, socket. r is a set of rights: read, write, execute, delete.

blocks.where: D is the domain; each pair names an object and its rights; {} means no access.

blocks.text: Static domains are fixed at start; simple but coarse. Dynamic domains change as the process runs, each change by a rule. Rights belong to the domain, not the pid, so the kernel stores a pointer to it.
A switch happens only through an entry point set up by someone with authority.
new domain = switch(old domain, object, right)
blocks.where: object is the program or file called; right permits the call; the result is the domain afterwards.

items: setuid exec. The file means 'run as owner'; on exec the process enters the owner's domain.
sudo. Password check, then one command in the root domain.
Guarded procedure. A user process calls a fixed entry point; hardware switches to a privileged ring. MULTICS had 8 rings; x86 has 4, ring 0 kernel, ring 3 user.

blocks.text: The kernel saved old rights at the entry point and restores them on return from the trap; the user takes no action.

sections.h3: UNIX maps a domain to (uid, gid)

blocks.text: In UNIX a domain is (uid, gid) plus supplementary groups. File mode bits give read, write and execute to owner, group, others. A uid 1000 process reads a 644 file owned by uid 1000, but gets only 'other' bits on a file owned by uid 0. exec of a setuid file replaces the effective uid for the life of the new image. The kernel records the old uid in the saved set-user-id, so the program can call setuid(1000) to drop back and setuid(0) to regain root while running.

figure.caption: Running passwd moves the child from D1 (uid 1000) to D2 (uid 0), where it may write /etc/shadow. The saved uid 1000 lets it drop back with setuid(1000); the shell stays in D1 throughout.

spec.aria: Two domain boxes, D1 for uid 1000 with no right on /etc/shadow and D2 for uid 0 with read and write on it, joined by an exec arrow one way and a dashed setuid(1000) arrow back.

examples.question: uid 1000, gid 1000 runs /usr/bin/passwd (setuid root). Before, the process may read/write notes.txt but not /etc/shadow. After, it can write /etc/shadow. Write both domains and say how it returns to the first.
steps: D1: notes.txt {read, write}; /usr/bin/passwd {read, execute}; /etc/shadow {}; uid 1000, gid 1000.
exec sees the setuid bit on /usr/bin/passwd; effective uid becomes 0. That is the switch.
D2: notes.txt {read, write}; /etc/shadow {read, write}; all files get uid 0 rights.

At exec the kernel recorded 1000 in the saved set-user-id. exec replaces the image, and effective uid is 0 for its life. The program may call setuid(1000) to drop to D1, then setuid(0) to return. When it finishes, the process ends; the parent shell stayed in D1.
The shell forked a child before exec; no exit restore is involved.
examples.answer: D1 = {(notes.txt, {read, write}), (/usr/bin/passwd, {read, execute}), (/etc/shadow, {})}; D2 = {(notes.txt, {read, write}), (/etc/shadow, {read, write}), (any file, uid 0 rights)}. The program drops back with setuid(1000) using the saved set-user-id, or simply ends; the parent shell never left D1.
examples.check:
uid_before = 1000
setuid_owner = 0
print(uid_before)          # shell
print(setuid_owner)        # child during exec
print(uid_before)          # shell unchanged

traps: A domain changes only by an explicit mechanism — setuid exec, sudo, ring switch. Reading a file changes nothing.
Rights belong to the domain, not the pid. Two processes in one domain hold identical rights.
setuid changes effective uid, not real uid. The saved set-user-id lets the program call setuid() to drop back or regain root; the kernel does not restore it on exit.
A system call trapping to a privileged ring is a domain switch; a library call in the same ring is not.

quiz.q: Define a domain and give its form.
quiz.a: A domain is the set of rights a process holds at a moment, written as pairs (object, set of rights).

quiz.q: Why is a static domain easier to check but less useful than a dynamic one?
quiz.a: A static domain never changes, so rights are checked once at creation. It is coarse: the process must hold its largest future set all the time, which violates least privilege.

quiz.q: Why can a process not simply set its own uid to 0?
quiz.a: Changing uid is a domain switch, allowed only through an authorised entry point: a setuid file, or sudo after a password check. A plain assignment is refused unless the process already has privilege.

quiz.q: A uid 1000 process runs a setuid root program and opens /etc/shadow for writing. Which domain holds that right, and which uid is checked?
quiz.a: The right sits in D2, entered at exec; the check uses effective uid 0. The program can drop to uid 1000 with setuid(1000) using the saved set-user-id, or the process simply ends; the parent shell remains in D1.

quiz.q: Two processes share one domain object. Process A execs a setuid program. Does B gain the new rights?
quiz.a: No. exec creates a new domain for A and attaches only A to it; B still points at the old domain object. Rights belong to the domain, so B is unchanged.

quiz.q: Why does a guarded procedure need a hardware trap, while a normal function call does not?
quiz.a: A normal call stays in ring 3 with the same rights, so nothing needs checking. Entering the kernel's domain changes rights; the caller must not choose its own entry point. The trap sends control to a fixed kernel address, which checks arguments, then returns to ring 3.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linux splits the (uid, gid) domain into capabilities such as CAP_NET_ADMIN, so one power can be held without root. Containers add namespaces and seccomp filters that shrink the domain. Windows uses restricted tokens and AppContainer identifiers. Object-capability systems go further: a domain is exactly the set of tickets it holds. Search next: Linux capabilities, seccomp-bpf, principle of least authority.
